title: Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory
lead: Light switched on at a given moment is a perturbation that changes with time. Dirac's method follows the amplitudes of the unperturbed states while the perturbation acts, and a system of two levels shows how a transition builds up.
notes: Adapted from Wikipedia and shared under CC BY-SA 4.0; a stray “{\displaystyle |j\rangle }” that the Wikipedia source left in the text is dropped.
exercise_notes: The one exercise was written by AI with an AI solution; its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: Diagram showing two states, |1⟩ and |2⟩, with a pink dashed arrow indicating a transition between them. Graph showing a curve with a peak around the value 1 on the t-axis and labeled axes for ω - ω₀ and t.

exercises.source_id: should turn off perturbation after time
exercises.prompt: Light is tuned $2.0\times10^{12}$ rad/s away from the natural frequency of a two-level system, $|\omega - \omega_0| = 2.0\times10^{12}\ \text{s}^{-1}$, and its coupling is $|H_{21}|/\hbar = 2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{s}^{-1}$. The system starts in $|1\rangle$. (a) After what time is the transition probability $P_{12}$ first at its largest? (b) What is $P_{12}$ then? (c) What would $P_{12}$ be after the same time if the light were exactly on resonance?

answer.solution:
(a) With $P_{12}(t) = \dfrac{|H_{21}|^2}{\hbar^2}\dfrac{\sin^2[(\omega-\omega_0)t/2]}{(\omega-\omega_0)^2}$, the sine squared first reaches 1 when $(\omega-\omega_0)t/2 = \pi/2$, so $t = \pi/|\omega-\omega_0| = \pi/(2.0\times10^{12}\ \text{s}^{-1}) = 1.571\times10^{-12}$ s, or 1.571 ps.

(b) There the probability is $\left(\dfrac{|H_{21}|/\hbar}{|\omega-\omega_0|}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{2.0\times10^{11}}{2.0\times10^{12}}\right)^2 = 0.0100$. Off resonance the upper state never holds more than this, however long the light stays on.

(c) At resonance the limit of the sine over its argument gives $P_{12} = \left(\dfrac{|H_{21}|t}{2\hbar}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{(2.0\times10^{11}\ \text{s}^{-1})(1.571\times10^{-12}\ \text{s})}{2}\right)^2 = (0.157)^2 = 0.0247$, two and a half times as much, and still growing as $t^2$.

footnotes.html: “Permutation” means perturbation: these are the matrix elements of $H_1(t)$.
The book's graph labels its axis $t$, but it plots $P_{12}$ against $\omega - \omega_0$ at one time; its peak of 0.25 is $\sin^2(x/2)/x^2$ at $x = 0$, for $t = 1$.

assumes.text: The perturbation $\kV(\kt)$ is the perturbing Hamiltonian $\kHone(\kt)$.

steps.cap: $\partial/\partial t$ acts by a chain rule on the product $c_n(t)e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$, and the derivative of the phase brings down $-iE_n/\hbar$.
The terms in $c_nE_n$ stand on both sides and cancel.
Resolving the identity in front of $V$: taking the product with $\langle k|$ keeps only the $k$ term of the derivatives, by orthonormality, and leaves the matrix elements of the perturbation.

derivations.what: the transition probability of a two-level system

assumes.tex: i \hbar \dfrac{\partial c_2(\kt)}{\partial \kt} = c_2(\kt) H_{22}(\kt) + c_1 e^{+i \komegazero \kt} H_{21} (\kt)

assumes.text: The system starts in $|1\rangle$, so $c_1(0) = 1$ and $c_2(0) = 0$.

steps.cap: To first order the right side keeps the starting amplitudes, $c_1 = 1$, and $H_{22} = 0$ removes the other term.

nodes.note: The book writes the exponential under the integral over $t'$ as $e^{i\omega_o t}$; it is $e^{i\omega_0 t'}$.

steps.cap: From here $H_{21}$ is the matrix element of the amplitude $V(r)$, the part that does not change in time.
Near resonance the first exponential turns many times while the second barely moves, so the first integral stays small and is dropped.
Take out half the phase: $e^{ix} - 1 = e^{ix/2}\left(e^{ix/2} - e^{-ix/2}\right) = 2i\,e^{ix/2}\sin(x/2)$.
The sine is odd, so $\sin(-x)/(-y) = \sin x/y$.

nodes.note: The book prints $c_2(t) = - \dfrac{2i}{\hbar} \dfrac{\sin (\omega-\omega_o)t /2}{ (\omega-\omega_o )t} e^{i (\omega_0-\omega)t/2} H_{21}$, with an extra $t$ in the denominator and a factor $2i$ too many; its own peak height, $|H_{12}t/2\hbar|^2$, agrees with the form here.

assumes.text: The square of the absolute amplitude $c_n(t)$ is the probability that the system is in state $n$ at time $t$.

nodes.note: The book prints $P_{12}(t) = \dfrac{4}{\hbar^2} \left| \dfrac{\sin (\omega-\omega_o)t /2}{ (\omega-\omega_o )t} \right|^2 | H_{21} |^2$, which differs from this by a factor $4/t^2$.
